description: We are Girls Who Code at BCC. Our team is interested in games, web dev, and space. This is the 2nd team branch which is focusing on the Space Mission.
summary:
2D mission game where we explore different planets survival elements with NPCs. We walk around the spaceship then we are tasks to help out NPCs and upgrade the ship to not fail the mission. Each playthrough is unique and has procedurally generated rooms for the player to play so they will never run out of things to do in a run. 

A realistic space mission game depends on real science at every step. A mission starts with a scientific need, is limited by its budget, is built and run by many specialists, faces risks that NASA ranks and studies, must supply life support to keep astronauts alive, and leaves lasting effects on the people who fly it. The challenge resources add practical tools for building the game: the General Mission Analysis Tool for modeling trajectories, and NASA's web-based mission visualization tools for showing them. Using these facts as rules, limits, and consequences can help a player learn that every mission design choice is a trade-off.

This game starts the way real missions do, with the player choosing a scientific objective. We modeled this game after some of the other resources. For example, "Learning Game About Telescopes" resource shows how: the player's science goals limit which instruments and wavelengths are available, and some options are blocked when they don't fit the objectives. The same resource uses three levels of increasing difficulty, so that more ambitious goals require more complex engineering.
details:
Introduction

The 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge "Space Mission Design Game" asks teams to build an interactive game in which players design, manage, and simulate a complete space mission. Players make engineering decisions, manage limited resources, and see how each choice shapes the success of the mission [1]. Designing a real mission means balancing many competing demands, including mission objectives, spacecraft design, scientific instruments, launch vehicles, budgets, power, mass, communications, and orbital limits [1].

Our game is made to reflect what a real mission aboard a Nasa mission would be like while simultaneously educating users on what goes on behind the scenes of the space ships through interactive player movement and survival mechanics. The goal of the game is for players to complete a mission to land on a planet while navigating the harsh conditions of space.

For a game like this to teach anything, its rules must come from real science. This summary researches the real-world facts behind the game, using NASA's own data and the resources listed on the challenge page. It follows the order of a mission and answers six questions: why a mission happens, how much it costs, who works on it, what risks astronauts face, what astronauts need to survive and how life support provides it, and what happens to astronauts' bodies after they return. Each section ends with what the finding means for the game.

1. Why the Mission?

Every space mission begins with a scientific need. NASA's systems-engineering approach takes a mission from that first need through requirements definition, design, verification, and implementation [2]. NASA also uses Concept Maturity Levels (CMLs), a framework developed by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, to measure how developed a mission idea is before formal project work begins [2]. The levels start with CML 1, an initial mission idea, and move through feasibility analysis, trade studies, point design, implementation planning, and detailed engineering. The greatest design decisions are made in CML 1 to 4 [2].

NASA's Mission Design Lab at Goddard Space Flight Center supports this early work. It is a collaborative engineering environment where engineers and science partners develop mission concepts [3]. The lab's study levels range from quick brainstorming, to feasibility and risk assessment, to trade studies, to a detailed point design [2].

What this means for the game: The game should start the way real missions do, with the player choosing a scientific objective. For example, "Learning Game About Telescopes" resource shows how: the player's science goals limit which instruments and wavelengths are available, and some options are blocked when they don't fit the objectives [2]. The same resource uses three levels of increasing difficulty, so that more ambitious goals require more complex engineering [2].

2. The Budget

Money limits every mission. At the Mission Design Lab, the most detailed study level, called a point design, produces CAD models, equipment lists, engineering models, and cost estimates [2][3]. NASA's work is paid for through the yearly federal budget, and the agency publishes its budget request documents online [8][9].

The numbers for fiscal year 2026 show how much a budget can change. The President's request for NASA was $18.8 billion, and it proposed cutting International Space Station funding to $920 million [15]. Later reporting says Congress approved about $24.4 billion [14]. The first figure is a proposal and the second appears to be the approved amount, so a final paper should confirm the current number on NASA's budget page [8].

What this means for the game: Budget should be the main limited resource. Because real teams compare options in trade studies [2], the game can make players choose between designs, such as a cheaper spacecraft with fewer instruments or a costlier one with more capability, and show the cost of each choice.

3. Who Works on the Spaceship?

A mission is a team effort. The challenge resources divide a mission into four segments. The launch segment provides the launch vehicle and services. The space segment is the spacecraft, instruments, orbiters, landers, or rovers. The ground segment is the ground stations and mission-control facilities that handle communication, data reception, and mission management. The user segment is the scientists and other users who analyze and apply the data [2].

Many specialists support the design itself. In the Mission Design Lab, engineers and science partners work together on a concept [3]. The lab looks at the whole mission, including orbit and trajectory, spacecraft systems, communications, ground systems, launch vehicle, and operations, as well as power, propulsion, thermal control, structures, avionics, software, reliability, cost, and risk [2]. For crewed spacecraft, engineers at NASA's Marshall and Johnson centers develop and test the life support systems [7].

What this means for the game: The four segments can become the game's team roles or mission sections, so the player has to staff and fund the ground and science sides as well as the spacecraft.

4. Risks

Risk is part of mission design from the start. The Mission Design Lab's concept development level assesses both feasibility and risk [2]. For missions with astronauts, NASA's Human Research Program names five main hazards of spaceflight: radiation, altered gravity, isolation and confinement, closed environments, and distance from Earth [4]. These hazards are linked to more than 30 specific health risks [4].

NASA ranks these risks by how likely they are and how serious the consequences would be [4]. Its highest-priority "red" risks for exploration missions include health effects of space radiation, changes to the eyes and brain called Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), declines in behavioral health and performance, and inadequate food and nutrition [4]. NASA's risk pages also list changes to the immune system, bone changes, and the effects of stress, isolation, and teamwork problems on crew mental health [5].

What this means for the game: Random events in the game could be built from this list, with more likely or more serious risks having bigger effects. A longer or farther mission should raise the risk, because distance from Earth and mission length are themselves hazards [4].

5. What Astronauts Need and How Life Support Helps Them Live

Astronauts need air to breathe, water to drink, a safe pressure and temperature, and a way to deal with waste. NASA's Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) maintains a habitable, life-sustaining environment for the crew [6]. On the International Space Station, life support must supply oxygen and remove carbon dioxide, and it must also keep gases such as ammonia and acetone, which people give off in small amounts, from building up [7]. The primary source of oxygen on the station is electrolysis of water [7]. NASA uses the station as a testbed so that proven life support technologies can support future deep-space missions [6].

What this means for the game: Life support should be a required part of any crewed design. It uses mass, power, and budget, so a player who skimps on it should face higher risk, and a player who adds more should have less left for science instruments.

6. After the Mission: Changes When Astronauts Come Back

The effects of spaceflight continue after landing. NASA's Human Research Program studies changes to the immune system, to the structure of the eyes and brain, and to the bones [5]. NASA's Human Health Countermeasures group works to understand these physical effects and to develop ways to reduce the harmful ones [12]. A review of NASA's evidence reports noted that studying long-term health outcomes, those that appear after an astronaut retires, would be valuable [10].

What this means for the game: The end-of-mission screen should show results in two parts: the science the mission achieved and the health cost to the crew. After the game launches the player's design, the telescope resource already shows how this can work. It presents the finished spacecraft, gives scientific results, and links the player's design to similar real NASA missions [2].

1. Hardware and Software the Game

Godot, Github, and Visual studios were integral to the backend of our game (no AI coding was used in the making of this game). Pixel studio was used to make all original art, backgrounds, and animations (no AI art was used in the making of this game).

Conclusion

A realistic space mission game depends on real science at every step. A mission starts with a scientific need, is limited by its budget, is built and run by many specialists, faces risks that NASA ranks and studies, must supply life support to keep astronauts alive, and leaves lasting effects on the people who fly it. The challenge resources add practical tools for building the game: the General Mission Analysis Tool for modeling trajectories [2], and NASA's web-based mission visualization tools for showing them [11]. Using these facts as rules, limits, and consequences can help a player learn that every mission design choice is a trade-off.
